claim: WSTS describes itself as a non-profit organization of semiconductor product companies founded in 1986 and as the industry's only source for monthly industry shipment statistics.
evidence: "World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) was founded in 1986 as a non-profit organization of semiconductor product companies and is the industry's only source for monthly industry shipment statistics." (About WSTS, Spring 2026 release, 2 June 2026)

claim: A company may become a WSTS member only if it at least designs and sells semiconductor products under its own trade name, and members are obliged to report their revenue data regularly to WSTS's Data Collection Agents.
evidence: "A company that at least designs and sells semiconductor products under its own trade name may become WSTS member." ... "Membership both comprises the obligation to feed the member company's revenue data regularly into the appointed Data Collection Agents." (WSTS Overview page)

claim: WSTS market statistics cover worldwide semiconductor shipments in 205 product categories by revenue and 241 product categories by units.
evidence: "Worldwide semiconductor shipments covering 205 product categories by revenue and 241 product categories by units" (WSTS Market Statistics page)

claim: WSTS monthly market statistics report five regions: Americas, Europe, Japan, China and Asia Pacific/All Other; end-use data are published yearly.
evidence: "the regions Americas, Europe, Japan, China and Asia Pacific/All Other" (WSTS Market Statistics page); page lists End Use data as a yearly report (paraphrase of the report-frequency list on the same page)

claim: WSTS's published market forecast tables use four regions (Americas, Europe, Japan, Asia Pacific), in which China is not shown separately.
evidence: paraphrase: regional table in the Spring 2026 forecast release lists Americas, Europe, Japan and Asia Pacific only (release of 2 June 2026, regional table)

claim: SIA's monthly global semiconductor sales figures are WSTS-compiled data expressed as a three-month moving average.
evidence: paraphrase of methodology note: monthly sales data compiled by the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) organization represent a three-month moving average (SIA release, 4 Sept 2026, footer)

claim: SIA states that it represents 99% of the U.S. semiconductor industry by revenue and nearly two-thirds of non-U.S. chip firms.
evidence: "The Semiconductor Industry Association represents 99% of the U.S. semiconductor industry by revenue and nearly two-thirds of non-U.S. chip firms." (SIA release, 4 Sept 2026, About SIA)

claim: In the U.S. International Trade Administration's 2016 semiconductor report, company market-share data were based on the headquarters of the seller, with foundry output not included and fabless companies included.
evidence: Figure 1 note: "headquarters of seller" ... "Foundry output not included, fabless included" (ITA 2016 Top Markets Report, Executive Summary, Figure 1 note)

claim: Pure-play foundry wafer revenue is unlikely to be counted as a separate population in the WSTS headline market, because WSTS reporting is by companies selling chips under their own trade name; chips made by foundries are counted when sold by their (fabless) customers.
evidence: Reasoning from WSTS membership criterion and ITA note that foundry output is not included while fabless is.
notes: Based on c_wsts_member and c_ita_hq. WSTS's public pages do not state foundry treatment explicitly; needs confirmation (see interview queue).

claim: The U.S. ITA noted that overseas packaging, final assembly and transshipments skew semiconductor import and export data, making trade statistics a poor measure of where chips are made or consumed.
evidence: "It was difficult in the case of semiconductors, however, due to overseas packaging and final assembly of semiconductors and transshipments skewing the import and export data." (ITA 2016 Top Markets Report, Executive Summary)

claim: WSTS defines reportable semiconductor products as either packaged/encapsulated die or chips that are tested and marked, or unencapsulated die, chips or wafers that have been tested to product specifications.
evidence: "Semiconductor Products are defined in two forms: 1. Packaged or encapsulated die or chips with leads or contacts, which are tested and marked (or identified) to meet the product specifications (finished products). 2. Die, chips or wafers, which have not been encapsulated but have been tested to meet the product specifications and are identified by the container or package in which they are shipped." (WSTS Product Classification 2021, p. 3)

claim: WSTS counts chip development charges such as non-recurring engineering (NRE) charges for custom and semi-custom devices as part of reported semiconductor value.
evidence: "Chip development charges, such as non-recurring engineering (NRE) charges for custom and semi-custom devices, are part of the value to be reported." (WSTS Product Classification 2021, p. 9)

claim: The WSTS classification has four top-level product groups: discretes, optoelectronics, sensors and actuators, and integrated circuits; integrated circuits are split into analog, MOS micro, logic and memory.
evidence: paraphrase: section 3.1 Discretes (p. 4-6), 3.2 Optoelectronics (p. 6-7), 3.3 Sensors and Actuators (p. 7), 3.4 Integrated Circuits with Analog (p. 7-13), MOS Micro (p. 13-17), Logic (p. 17-21), Memory (p. 21-24) (WSTS Product Classification 2021)

claim: In the WSTS classification, MOS Micro comprises microprocessors (MPU), microcontrollers (MCU) and digital signal processors (DSP), and Memory comprises DRAM, SRAM, flash and ROM/EPROM types.
evidence: paraphrase: MOS Micro section (p. 13-17) lists MPU, MCU, DSP; Memory section (p. 21-24) lists DRAM, SRAM, Flash, ROM/EPROM (WSTS Product Classification 2021)

claim: WSTS optoelectronics excludes liquid crystal devices and displays and incandescent lamps, so LCD panels are outside the WSTS semiconductor market (display driver ICs are counted under logic).
evidence: "Includes displays, lamps, couplers, and other opto-sensing and emitting semiconductor devices (excludes liquid crystal devices and displays, incandescent lamps and displays, etc.)." (WSTS Product Classification 2021, p. 6); display drivers appear as MOS Display Drivers in the Logic section (paraphrase, p. 17-21)

claim: Whether solar (photovoltaic) cells are included in the WSTS semiconductor market could not be established from the public 2021 WSTS Product Classification.
evidence: Searched the WSTS Product Classification 2021 (SIA-hosted PDF) for 'solar', 'photovoltaic' and 'PV'; the document tool reported no occurrences. Newer classification (2023) is behind SIA subscriber login.

claim: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 (Manufacture of electronic components and boards) groups integrated circuits, microprocessors, diodes and transistors and semiconductor wafers together with electronic capacitors, resistors, inductors, connectors, bare printed circuit boards, LCD/plasma display components, LEDs and the loading of components onto printed circuit boards.
evidence: "manufacture of capacitors, electronic" ... "manufacture of resistors, electronic" ... "manufacture of bare printed circuit boards" ... "manufacture of integrated circuits" ... "manufacture of diodes, transistors and related discrete devices" ... "manufacture of dice or wafers, semiconductor" ... "manufacture of display components (plasma, polymer, LCD)" ... "manufacture of light emitting diodes (LED)" ... "loading of components onto printed circuit boards." (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 2610, 'This class includes')

claim: ISIC Rev.4 class 2610 excludes manufacture of computer and television displays and printing of smart cards; complete equipment is classified elsewhere.
evidence: "printing of smart cards"; "manufacture of computer and television displays"; "manufacture of complete equipment is classified elsewhere based on complete equipment classification" (UNSD ISIC Rev.4 2610, 'This class excludes')

claim: The Canadian NAICS 2022 industry 334410 (Semiconductor and other electronic component manufacturing) lists as illustrative examples electronic capacitors, integrated microcircuits, solar cells, printed circuit laminates, semiconductor wafers, transistors and loaded computer boards.
evidence: "capacitors, electronic, fixed and variable, manufacturing"; "integrated microcircuits, manufacturing"; "solar cells, manufacturing"; "printed circuit laminates, manufacturing"; "semiconductor devices (e.g., wafers), manufacturing"; "transistors, manufacturing"; "loaded computer boards, manufacturing" (Statistics Canada, NAICS 2022 v1.0, 334410 illustrative examples)

claim: Official industrial classifications (ISIC 2610, NAICS 334410) define a wider population than the industry-body 'semiconductor market': they bundle semiconductors with passive components, printed circuit boards and (in NAICS) solar cells, so official production and employment statistics are not directly comparable with WSTS sales figures.
evidence: Our reading of c_isic_incl, c_naicsca versus c_wsts_top / c_wsts_opto_excl.
notes: US NAICS 6-digit 334413 (Semiconductor and Related Device Manufacturing) is narrower but its official text could not be retrieved (census.gov pages render via JavaScript).

claim: The Harmonized System (Chapter 85, Note 12) defines semiconductor devices as devices whose operation depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field, or semiconductor-based transducers.
evidence: "Semiconductor devices are semiconductor devices the operation of which depends on variations in resistivity on the application of an electric field or semiconductor-based transducers." (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12(a))

claim: For customs purposes (HS heading 8542), electronic integrated circuits comprise monolithic, hybrid, multichip and multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs).
evidence: paraphrase: Note 12(b) defines four categories: monolithic integrated circuits ("circuit elements...are created in the mass (essentially) and on the surface of a semiconductor"), hybrid integrated circuits, multichip integrated circuits and multi-component integrated circuits (MCOs) (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12(b))

claim: The Harmonized System classifies light-emitting diodes as semiconductor devices.
evidence: "Light-emitting diodes (LED) are semiconductor devices based on semiconductor materials which convert electrical energy into visible, infra-red or ultra-violet rays" (Schedule B 2022, Chapter 85, Note 12(a)(ii))

claim: The U.S. CHIPS statute defines eligible 'covered entities' by facilities for fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production or R&D of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment, so U.S. policy treats equipment and materials as part of the semiconductor industry.
evidence: "...a facility relating to fabrication, assembly, testing, advanced packaging, production, or research and development of semiconductors, materials used to manufacture semiconductors, or semiconductor manufacturing equipment." (15 U.S.C. 4651(2))

claim: The U.S. CHIPS statute does not itself define 'semiconductor' or 'mature technology node'; both have the meaning given by the Secretary of Commerce.
evidence: paraphrase: the terms 'semiconductor' (para. 13) and 'mature technology node' (para. 10) are defined as having "the meaning given" by the Secretary (15 U.S.C. 4651)

claim: U.S. Commerce regulations define a semiconductor as an integrated electronic device or system most commonly manufactured using materials such as silicon, silicon carbide or III-V compounds.
evidence: "An integrated electronic device or system most commonly manufactured using materials such as silicon, silicon carbide, or III-V compounds" (15 CFR 231.115)

claim: U.S. Commerce regulations define semiconductor manufacturing as three stages: wafer production, semiconductor fabrication and semiconductor packaging.
evidence: paraphrase: 'Semiconductor manufacturing' includes "semiconductor wafer production, semiconductor fabrication or semiconductor packaging" (15 CFR 231.116)

claim: U.S. CHIPS guardrail regulations define 'legacy' fabrication as digital/analog logic at the 28-nanometer generation or older, DRAM with half-pitch above 18 nm, or NAND flash with fewer than 128 layers; legacy wafer production covers silicon wafers of 200 mm or smaller.
evidence: paraphrase of 15 CFR 231.107(a): wafer production — silicon wafers 8 inches (200 mm) or smaller, compound wafers 6 inches or smaller; fabrication — logic at 28-nanometer generation or older, DRAM half-pitch greater than 18 nm, NAND below 128 layers; packaging — without advanced 3D integration packaging

claim: Under U.S. CHIPS guardrail regulations, chips using post-planar transistor architectures (such as FinFET or gate-all-around) or advanced 3D integration packaging are not legacy semiconductors.
evidence: paraphrase of 15 CFR 231.107(b): semiconductors critical to national security, those with post-planar transistor architectures and those using advanced 3D integration packaging are not legacy semiconductors

evidence: "Note: Military end-use is included in Government. Sources: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS)." (SIA 2025 Factbook, Section 2, p. 8)

claim: In 2023 the PC/computer end market fell to 25% of semiconductor sales while communications' share rose 2 percentage points and automotive became the third-largest end market, per the WSTS End-Use Survey.
evidence: "Sales to the communications industry, however, increased by 2 percentage points while the PC/computer decreased to 25% of sales." ... "the automotive sector experienced the largest growth in share of chip sales to become the third-largest end market in 2023." (SIA, 18 Mar 2024)

evidence: "In 2024, the U.S. semiconductor industry continued that trend, with U.S. headquartered companies reaching sales of $318 billion, accounting for 50.4% of global sales revenue." (SIA State of the Industry 2025, p. 23)

claim: SIA's value-chain shares for EDA, design, manufacturing equipment and raw materials are based on company revenues attributed to company headquarters location.
evidence: "EDA, design, manufacturing equipment, and raw materials based on company revenues and company headquarters location." (SIA State of the Industry 2025, p. 20, note)

claim: Two incompatible regional conventions coexist: WSTS regional market data describe where chips are sold (e.g. Americas US$256.5bn in 2025), while 'industry share' figures attribute sales to the seller's headquarters country (e.g. U.S.-HQ firms 50.4% of global sales in 2024).
evidence: Our reading of c_wsts25_amer, c_us_hq, c_hq_method and c_ita_hq.
notes: WSTS's exact regional attribution basis (ship-to vs bill-to) is not publicly stated; see interview queue.

claim: In the SIA Factbook's regional market chart, China data are a subset of the Asia Pacific market, whereas SIA monthly releases report China and 'Asia Pacific/All Other' as separate regions.
evidence: "In this graph, the China market data from 2014-2024 represents a subset of the overall Asia Pacific Market" (SIA 2025 Factbook, Section 2, p. 10); SIA July 2026 release lists Asia Pacific/All Other and China separately (paraphrase)

claim: The basis on which WSTS attributes sales to regions (ship-to location, bill-to location, or customer headquarters) could not be established from public WSTS or SIA pages.
evidence: Checked WSTS Overview and Market Statistics pages, SIA monthly release footers (Sept 2026), SIA 2025 Factbook; none states the attribution rule.

claim: How WSTS accounts for sales of non-member companies (and hence what share of the world market is directly reported) is not disclosed on its public pages.
evidence: Checked WSTS Overview and Market Statistics pages and the About WSTS text in forecast releases (2025-2026); no statement found.

claim: SIA and BCG use 'DAO' to group discretes, analog, and optoelectronics and sensors, and segment wafer-fab capacity into DRAM, NAND, logic by node (<10nm, 10-22nm, 28nm and above) and DAO.
evidence: "DAO: Discretes, analog, and optoelectronics & sensors" (slide 6, footnote 1); capacity chart categories DRAM, NAND, Logic <10nm, 10-22nm, 28nm+, DAO (paraphrase, slide 6) (SIA/BCG briefing deck, 2024)

claim: SIA and BCG found more than 50 points across the semiconductor value chain where one region holds more than 65% of global market share.
evidence: "more than 50 points across the value chain where one region holds more than 65% of the global market share" (SIA/BCG 2021 two-page summary)

claim: Process-node names such as '14 nm' or '22 nm' no longer correspond to any specific physical dimension on the chip.
evidence: "I'm the first to admit that I can't point to the one dimension that's 32 nm or 22 nm or 14 nm. Some dimensions are smaller than the stated node name, and others are larger." — Mark Bohr, Intel senior fellow (IEEE Spectrum, 28 Oct 2013)

claim: Samsung describes the semiconductor ecosystem as made up of integrated device manufacturers (IDMs), fabless designers, foundries, design houses, OSATs (outsourced assembly and test) and IP companies.
evidence: IDM: "Corporations that handles all processes in manufacturing semiconductors"; OSAT: "Takes clients in to package and test semiconductors"; plus sections on Fabless, Foundry, Design House, IP Companies (Samsung Semiconductor tech blog, 22 June 2023)

claim: The headline 'semiconductor market' (~US$0.8 trillion in 2025) counts only chip sales; equipment (US$135bn), materials (US$73bn) and EDA/IP (~US$5.5bn per quarter) are measured by different bodies as separate markets and are inputs to, not part of, that figure.
evidence: Our reading of c_wsts25, c_semieq, c_semimat, c_esd and WSTS product definition c_wsts_form.
notes: Adding these together would double count: equipment and materials costs are embedded in chip prices.
